title: Controls Leader PCB — LHR Solar Car
role: Vehicle Controls & Telemetry (VCAT) Engineer, Longhorn Racing Solar
hook: The solar car's central nervous system — 15+ driver inputs buffered onto 3 CAN buses by a custom STM32L4 board.
summary: Custom STM32L4-based PCB serving as the solar car's central hub for all driver-dashboard and steering wheel inputs — 15+ functions buffered and transmitted over 3 CAN bus lines at 500 kbps via thread-safe FreeRTOS firmware.
description: Designed a custom PCB that acts as the central hub for human-machine interface inputs on UT Austin's Longhorn Racing solar car. The board interfaces 15+ driver-dashboard functions and GPIO inputs — ignition, gear selection, cruise control, regen, hazards, turn indicators, and horn — with an STM32L4 MCU, transmitting all buffered signals across 3 CAN bus lines at 500 kbps to every peripheral board through a thread-safe FreeRTOS code structure. Built a protected 24V→5V→3.3V power system with buck/LDO stages, reverse-polarity protection, and consistent noise filtering for reliable operation in any environment, plus isolated power and ground dedicated to the dual CAN transceiver interfaces. Developed MOSFET-based input protection and op-amp buffer circuits to isolate sensors from the MCU GPIOs, minimizing current draw and ensuring clean, debounced signal acquisition. Collaborated with mechanical teams to meet packaging requirements, iterating through RevA/RevB hardware revision cycles with schematic reviews and design rule checks, while co-developing low-level C firmware for real-time signal handling.

title: Pedals Board PCB — LHR Solar Car
role: Vehicle Controls & Telemetry (VCAT) Engineer, Longhorn Racing Solar
hook: Turns pedal presses into data — redundant analog brake & throttle sensing feeding an STM32G4 over CAN.
summary: Custom STM32G4-based PCB reading brake & accelerator pedal inputs and brake-line pressure — buffered analog signals, redundant sensing paths, and processed data transmitted over CAN.
description: Designed a custom PCB that interfaces the solar car's brake and accelerator pedal inputs and measures brake-line pressure, buffering the analog signals before feeding them into an STM32G4's ADC inputs and transmitting the processed data over CAN. The board is a pedal daughter board that mates with the Peripheral Sensing/Output Module (PSOM) to sense linear potentiometers and the brake-line pressure sensor. Integrated UART debugging for thorough system testing of each ADC input and its data processing in real time, enabling both hardware- and software-level signal verification. Leveraged redundant sensing paths and signal shielding to improve data integrity and reduce the impact of noise and EMI on safety-critical control signals.

title: VCU PCB — LHR Solar Car
role: Vehicle Controls & Telemetry (VCAT) System Lead, Longhorn Racing Solar
hook: The solar car's motor-control brain — a fully galvanically isolated CAN and signal interface that fixed the motor controller's EMI noise.
summary: Motor-control VCU for UT's 2026-27 solar car. A fully galvanically isolated CAN and signal interface fixed EMI and noise coupling into the motor controller, and a 100+ state FreeRTOS state machine runs BPS, motor-fault, and regen/cruise logic.
description: Designed the Vehicle Control Unit (VCU) for motor control on UT Austin's 2026-27 Longhorn Racing Solar car, as part of the Vehicle Controls & Telemetry (VCAT) system I lead. The motor controller was suffering from EMI and noise coupling, so the board is built around a fully galvanically isolated CAN and signal interface: an isolated motor CAN bus, an isolated SPI DAC that generates the accelerator and brake reference voltages, isolated digital mode and map signals, and a dedicated isolated supply for the motor side. MOSFET level shifting translates the map-bit, forward/reverse, and power/eco mode signals, and the motor's RPM pulse output is stepped down for the microcontroller. The vehicle side has a protected 12V input with a fuse and a buck regulator, a power mux that switches between the buck supply and USB power, and a 3.3V rail. Two CAN buses (car and motor) have transient protection and jumper-selectable bus termination, and the board also carries a microSD card, I2C dual-fan control with tach feedback, a thermistor input, fault and status LEDs, a USB-C port, and CAN debug headers and test points. On the software side, I wrote the STM32 FreeRTOS firmware as a 100+ state finite state machine with O(1) dispatch that runs BPS, motor-fault, and regen/cruise logic.

title: ROS2 & Gazebo Robotics Simulation
summary: Simulated a custom robot in ROS2 and Gazebo with sensor integration, control, and navigation — intermediate proficiency reached in under 3 weeks.
description: Designed and simulated a custom robot in ROS2 and Gazebo, utilizing the publish-subscribe model for sensor integration, control, and navigation. I pursued this project after my senior year (graduated high school) as a continuation of my ISM dog robot project seen in the project tile below. I wanted to run simulations of my dog robot with an industry-certified tool like ROS2. In just under 3 weeks I accomplished an intermediate level of proficiency in the ROS2 framework, and its methods of communication with simulators like RViz and Gazebo through Udemy certifications. Future Plans: During my freshman year as an ECE Honors major at UT Austin, I plan to implement the 3D .stl model of my robot design into Gazebo and start programming its limbs and test its movement virtually before running the ROS2 framework on the real bot.

Sensor integration, control and navigation
Intermediate ROS2 proficiency in under 3 weeks

title: DIY Hand Crank Generator
summary: After learning about electromagnetic induction from Physics 2, tested the theory with a hand crank generator built from 3D-printed gears and coils, generating 1V of potential difference.
description: After learning about electromagnetic induction from my Physics 2 class, I went on to test the theory with my own hand crank generator. I modeled and 3D-printed two beveled gears, with the big gear having six magnets attached while three coils were stationary and in series to induce current. I was able to generate 1 V of potential difference.
